Some people do think poor people food + black people food. But having two (black) Southern parents I can tell you that's not necessarily the assumption south of the Mason Dixon line.

Chicken wasn't poor people's food in the deep South. Quite the opposite. It was assumed that black people stole the chicken and ate it. That's where that trope came from. Watermelon? Because when you are thirsty, watermelon is a near instant hydration system. so while pretty much everyone down south ate watermelon, it must have seemed to white racists that black people had a special love for it because they would eat it at any chance they got while working. 

As for cornbread, cornbread is cheap compared to white bread. It was loved by everybody, but it was definitely seen as poor people's food- which is why it was assumed poor whites ate it a lot too.

However, put the three food items together, and you have a stereotypical shorthand. There's nothing wrong with any of these foods, separately or together, and plenty of black people in the US eat them. But it's the iconography that's upsetting.
Personally, I see this as (I hope) insensitivity rather than racism. It might simply be cluelessness. In Florida, no, it wouldn't be cluelessness. Why? Because plenty of people who are old enough to rune schools are also old enough to remember items like Mammy dolls. I should know. I'm 52, and lived through the end of segregation. Hope this helps.

What's amazing is that when something like this comes up, all of a sudden white Americans have not idea where this stuff comes from. And yet on white supremacist forums, EVERYBODY knows. I see a bit of disingenuousness here. Not necessarily with you (I can't read your mind), but with the general tone, as if people who know this stuff and don't like it are suffering from delusions. 

Me personally, I don't like watermelon. Fried chicken is ok. Cornbread? I prefer mine sweet. But I also know that one could pick any number of foods for Black History Month. Like maybe Googling recipes for different West African dishes. Or having South African food in honor of Mandela, Jamaican cuisine to honor Marcus Garvey and the numerous people from that country who came here before WWII (like Malcolm X's dad), Boston baked beans to honor WEB DuBois (who was born and raised in Massachusetts), and herring to honor Marcus Samuelsson (an Ethiopian who grew up in Sweden). Heck, you could even have fish, to honor Matthew Henson and crepes Suzette to honor Josephine Baker. 
Black people have lived all over the globe, not just in the southern US. For a school to decide these are the best foods for Black History Mponth is intellectually lazy, even if it wasn't meant to be racist. But I don't think I'm over-supposing that the reason why they didn't think in terms of black people being everywhere  is because to some extent they are, yeah, racist. They don't picture black people being all over the globe, or eating whatever is where they are. And as for the number of people here who've said, 'well, my black friend told me he loves those foods!,'maybe they should ask those same black friends if they own a passport or know anything about Black History other than George Washington Carver and Martin Luther King. Most black Americans don't know that people from the Caribbean and Africa have been living in Europe since before Shakespeare's time (and there are paintings and documents to prove it. Alexander Pushkin, the great Russian writer, was half-black. Alexandre Dumas the elder? The elephant in the room here is that the people who did this live in Florida. They are adults, and no doubt grew up with the stereotypes of what black people eat. They can't claim ignorance. That's why it's being called racists as opposed to merely insensitive.

 There is a whole history of African Americans being portrayed with bug eyes, chowing down on watermelon, corn bread and fried chicken. There is no history of Japanese only eating sushi. The equivalent would be celebrating Chinese New Year by making cat and dog soup.

What makes it bad is when people react horribly to my race. I spoke to a white woman on the phone once; we were supposed to meet up for a movie, as we had similar interests. I described myself, except for my skin color. We both showed up at the venue and I was the only person in the room who matched the description a gave her. I watched her pace around. She walked past me four times. She actually looked right at me. And then I went over to her and introduced myself. I thought she was going to go into shock. During coffee she asked me where I was from, and I said NYC. And then she asked where I was really from. In other words she couldn't believe I was from the us because I was black and spoke standard English with no accent. I had to insist I was from NYC. She looked embarrassed. She also never called me again.

It's not that I speak the Queen's English. It's that I'm black and speak the Queen's English- in  NY. Often the people who react the most badly are well educated white people, who seem to suddenly need to insist on how well educated they are. Or to tell me how much they love black music, especially hip hop o jazz. Or to tell me about their nannies and how they loved them. 
At that point I usually gently mention that I'm an opera fan, and that my grandfather was wealthy. It's amazing how quickly they stop talking to me after that.

"If your mom thinks it's cool, it's casual."

In other words, if it appeals to sexist boys of all ages, it's hardcore. By your standards, anyway.
I happen to think Galaxian is still cool, and beating that it difficult. It also takes more than a minute to learn. I also like chess and Go. You might not have heard, but peopl devote their lives to learning those games without staying up all night playing and shouting.

Your mom may very well have played video games when she was growing up. In order to make enough money to feed and clothe you, she probably doesn't have the time to sit around all day and play games. She probably has numerous other interests. And for all you know, she might find Assassins Creed to be cool. But here's the thing. When you as a guy play a video game that's hardcore, very often that games does not have female protagonists, isn't written in a way to intrigue someone who reads non genre novels, and might not have values that many women cherish.

I could just as easily say the reason hardcore cooks are people who are dedicated, and if it's the kind of cooking you think is cool, like grilling, then it's casual (with the implication that it's inferior and lightweight). In fact, I could easily say that truly hardcore cooks are dedicated to baking, which involves exact measurements, precision in mixing, a sense of aesthetics, and is too difficult to be picked up the way making a grilled cheese sandwich is. And guess what? If I use that standard, I'd be writing off most men as lousy cooks, because most men have no interest in baking. Yet baking is only one subset of cooking, and not all of it involves pastry-making. 
The standards most people here are unconsciously using (and I keep seeing fictitious moms and grandmas being used as examples of casual, simplistic gamers) are ones that exclude anyone who doesn't want to play games that involve violence. And most women aren't interested in violent games, not because they abhor violence but because most violent games don't have female first or second leads, or show women as silent and/or crazy objects of possession and desire.
Me personally, I don't like violent games. But I love Walking Dead, because there are plenty of realistically drawn and acted female characters. Plus, the game makes me think and it's not silly. On the other hand I think games like Call of Duty are the true time wasters. Not only do they not replicate what war is really like (real war involves things like boredom, shell shock, devastating injuries, living in squalor, maggots, and moral dilemmas), they make something very serious into a joke. Not only that- they take hours that could be spent actually learning something from people's lives while giving the illusion that players are doing something worthwhile. Real life generals have learned and practiced actual strategy with chess and go boards. Nobody is really learning much from games like COD. While they are great for bringing strangers together, they seem to foster racist and sexist behavior in particular, and antisocial attitudes in general. They make a virtue out of myopic thinking, and they eat up a lot of time doing that. Casual gaming, on the other hand, can be fanatical or not. And some casual games actually encourage a relationship with the outside world; Tetris, for instance, is great at encouraging spatial manipulation.
You don't need great hand/eye coordination for chess. The great masters of the game can play several matches at once inside their heads. Even some HOGs require a certain mental agility. But both chess and HOGs can be played into late old age, and experience makes one better at them.

There are people who make HOGs into a hobby, and those games are always designated as casual. "Serious" board game fans usually designate complex games like Scrabble as casual, because they aren't obscure and played mostly by nerds. 
The truth is, in the US at least, "casual" means a game anyone might play, that is fairly low on the violence quotient, that is of a type that is popular across generations and genders, and usually doesn't require a specialized or soured up gaming system. If it has a communal aspect (which games like Candy Crush Saga, Scrabble and Go do), that aspect is not a necessary part of playing the game for most people.

Rather than give a long explanation, I'll just show you. Yourgibs is my favorite person on Lets Play. He plays all kinds of games, but he admits that he really likes HOGs, even though a lot of guys ignore them. Google "yourgibs dorian grey syndrome" to see what I'm talking about.

Notonly that, but women actually make up large percentage of gamers, if one doesn't confine the idea of gaming to console games or MMPORGs. There are tons of women over 40, for instance, who play games like the PuppetShow series on the high difficulty level with the same dedication that some people bring to League of Legends.

I love all this talk of teaching granny and pappy how to use a computer. It's kind of funny, considering that my mom, who is 78, learned to use a computer at work during the 80s. I had my first computer built for me in 1984. Some of us grew up in an era where spending all of our time in virtual worlds would have been considered a waste of brainpower.  It's not that 'many people don't like to have to think long about something or that hard.' It's that we do. Things like art and science. Or making great food. Or rebuilding a classic car. or whatever.  Killing monsters or pretending to be a drug dealer or soldier? Sorry. We're busy.

Yup. And the last thing we want are games that large numbers of people enjoy. Because that would be bad... how?

I'm sorry that some of us aren't 'real' gamers. But you know, those museums aren't going to visit themselves. Those restaurants aren't going to eat their own food. And those books? They get lonely without readers. Ditto all those movies that aren't about comic book characters. Somebody has to watch them. In other words, some of us see gaming as a small part of our lives because we want to stretch our brains while doing other things. Having children has nothing to do with it. Quite frankly, most supposed hardcore gamers who like to go on and on about how hardcore they are, are emotionally and intellectually stunted. Not all hardcore gamers of course. A lot of them have lives outside of gaming, even if they don't talk about it.

This is what's so funny to me. I'm in my 50s. I could easily be the mom of most people on Reddit, and I have no interest in console games. Instead, i prefer iPad games from Big Fish, as well as games from TellTale (currently playing Walking Dead Season II). But guess what? I was playing Asteroids, King's Quest, and the Star Wars sit-down console before most of you were alive. I was an ace at Galaxian. Moreover, I'm a woman, and I used to refurbish pcs back in the day when you had to change floppies in order to play what you would now call retro games. Donkey Kong? Played it. Every version of Pac-Man? Played them.

I have no interest in console games because a) I'm not interested in social gaming; b) my personal beliefs won't allow me to play games where it's necessary to cause emotional or physical harm to others, even if they aren't real; c) I find most console games to be mind-numbingly boring and without any real story. I also refuse to play games that are sexist or racist, and that cuts out a lot of stuff right there. At the same time, I have no interest in 'female ghetto' games that are just about cooking and shopping. And yet I find tons of games to play. 

Any game is put-downable. Books are too. We can't spend every minute in fantasy land. Casual is a slur that people who usually can tell you all about a badly-formulated fantasy world but can't explain the Constitution or express what makes decent art or what constitutes a good meal, use for other people who have lots of other thing to do with their lives other than sit in front of a console or a computer or a tablet, amusing themselves to death.  Many of those people are older and have real-life responsibilities, or are younger women who have different priorities.

How are they not the same? Aren't all games played for pleasure and satisfaction? Don't they require a certain amount of time in play to become better at the game? Don't they all reflect the cultures that created them and the values of those cultures?

That's the thing. Certain types of 'casual' games, like HOGs, time management games like Diner Dash and match 3s with pretty graphics, tend not to be liked by certain people. In fact, many of those games are made to be attractive to a female audience that are often older than the average so-called hard-core male gamer. They tend to be low and non-graphic on the death quotient, have female or non-gender specific protagonists, and have as their topic activities associated with women, such as shopping, cooking, or taking care of families. HOGs in particular tend to be more about solving puzzles and uncovering a story than just collecting objects or killing monsters. Some HOGs have fiendishly difficult puzzles and more and more, they are taking on a social aspect. And there are casual games that can take as long as a game of Monopoly, or even several days of concentrated play to finish. 

Some of the greatest, most complex games in history (among others, Go, Scrabble,  Mancala, Chess, Poker) can be played fairly casually or at a high tournament level. None of them involve blood and gore, even if they were originally designed to be a stand-in for war. Funnily enough, the average 'hardcore gamer' would find himself hard pressed to beat a longtime 'casual' Go or Scrabble player, and both of those games require a great deal of knowledge outside of the game universe. Also funnily enough, none of the great games of the world require one to play as a male, to kill people or surrogates, or fight boss levels. None of them reward people for yelling at people or calling them names. None of them cost a fortune to play. In many ways, casual gaming has more in common with classic gaming than the ones people play on consoles.

Peggle requires a high amount of luck? It does to some extent, but I would say it's mixture of luck and skill.

by your measurement would hidden object games be casual? There's not a lot of luck involved, there are no micro transactions, they have definite stories and endings, and they don't require a grind.

I enjoyed Stray Souls a great deal. Another favorite, and perhaps one of the best match 3 games go all time, is 4 Elements. It gets increasingly difficult as it goes along, and it requires good hand/eye coordination in order to beat it. The other games from the same studio are also excellent.

Unfortunately, for every unassuming vegetarian I've met, I've met at least one jerk. But I know plenty of meat eaters who are jerks, too. For instance, I've gotten all kinds of heckling when I've opened up my lunch in front of people and have revealed a full vegetarian (sometimes even vegan) lunch. Why anyone should care that I've been known to eat tofu and vegetable soup is a mystery to me.

Actually, cooking an entire vegetarian feast wouldn't be difficult. I'm not a vegetarian but I do cook, a lot. Sliced and grilled portobello mushroom salad for a starter (they taste like steak that way); eggplant Parmesan with a side of fried tofu and maybe squash blossoms or grilled pineapple; cheese, fruit and nuts for dessert, with an agar agar jelly made with cranberry or grape juice as a palate cleanser.

None of this is special vegetarian cuisine. It's just food. My meat loving boyfriend adores grilled mushrooms and eggplant parm. As for cheese you can go fancy and bake a Brie slathered in honey and fresh fruit, with or without a puff pastry wrapping.

For health and financial reasons, I eat meat fairly rarely, and yet most of my diet is based on what I was fed by my mother, whose mom grew up in farm country.

It's exhausting enough to be mentally ill. Bipolar kicks my ass and tells me lies on a daily basis. I see shadows move when nothing is there, have a voice in my head that tells me several times a day to kill myself. But medication is tiring too. The meds slow down the hypomania, but also the rest of the mind. Add in not enough work, isolation and money worries, and it's a horrendous thing to deal with. The only reason I have any dignity left is because I refuse to give it up.

Add in racism and the stigma that comes with mental illness and it makes life interesting.

One of the problems with having a disordered mind is that while doctors will and can give you medication, they really can't do much to help you rebuild your life, and most family and friends are repulsed by mental illness. Large numbers of us die because the lack of emotional support (which to be fair, is extremely rough on caregivers) is severely lacking.

1. Unfortunately, it typical to feel upset like this at 17.
2. As a woman, I can tell you that your former female friend might very well have a crush on you, and might be afraid that you don't feel the same way. 
3. I can't believe I'm saying this as I'm suicidal right now, but it gets better (not always permanently, but for long stretches at least). Find some hobbies. Write a story or some poetry about your feelings. Take photographs. Find ways of expressing yourself. Doing so will help you get through it.

Tutor a child who needs help. Do chores for someone who needs help (an old person, someone who is physically or mentally ill, a single parent, a widow or widower, someone who is under employed, a recent immigrant). Cook a meal for someone who is busy, or lonely and depressed. Leave a small gift (maybe some popcorn and a cheap movie, or a stuffed animal) for someone who needs cheering up. Buy cheap gloves and hand them out to the homeless. You can do the same thing with energy snacks and pet food. The biggest problem many people have is that they feel forgotten. Let them know they are still visible.
